name: Design MCP-ready ability names, side-effect annotations, and open-world distinction
query: We are designing WordPress abilities that will be exposed to MCP clients: (1) a generic `acme/manage-content` executor taking `action: create_draft | overwrite_post | delete_post | search_public_web`, (2) `acme/publish-post` which updates post status and fires a hook that sends subscriber email notifications, and (3) `acme/search-web` which queries a public web search API without modifying local or remote data. How should we structure the abilities, classify their side effects, and configure `meta.annotations` including `open_world`?
expected_behavior: Recommend splitting the generic executor into separate abilities with clear names, focused schemas, and descriptions when clients need individual MCP tools
Classify side effects across all execution paths, including fired hooks and delegated calls

Contrast an additive write such as creating a draft (`destructive: false`) with overwriting or deleting existing state (`destructive: true`), and explicitly call out irreversible side effects such as sending subscriber notifications
Explain that `readonly` and open-world are independent (the public web search ability can be both `readonly: true` and open-world)
Reference Core #66799 (`https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/66799`) without presenting `open_world` as an active core `meta.annotations` key before it lands
success_criteria: Replaces the generic executor with separate, individually callable abilities having clear names, focused schemas, and descriptions
Accounts for side effects in hooks and delegated calls when setting `readonly`, `destructive`, and `idempotent`
Distinguishes additive writes (draft creation) from state-overwriting/deleting writes and flags irreversible side effects (subscriber notifications)
States that read-only and open-world are independent using the public web search case
Links Core #66799 while noting `open_world` is not yet shipped in core `meta.annotations`
